summary: Describes how a network operator can ask for DNS servers to be delegated for the reverse lookup zone of a 6to4 IPv6 address block. The request uses an ordinary DNS delegation interface, and the requester is authenticated mainly by its source address and checked against the 6to4 prefix it owns. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Each site behind a 6to4 router needs its own entry in the DNS zone that maps addresses back to names. This memo describes the web service where a site asks for that entry and names the servers that will serve it.

questions: how does 6to4 reverse dns authenticate clients
subtitle: How a 6to4 site asks for DNS servers to be delegated for its own reverse lookup zone, with its source address as the proof.

tldr.problem: Reverse DNS lookups need a delegation path from the DNS root to the zone holding the PTR records, but 6to4 sites get their IPv6 addresses from their IPv4 address, so their upstream provider may offer no IPv6 at all and will not set up that delegation.
tldr.mechanism: A single zone, 2.0.0.2.ip6.arpa, is delegated only at the 48th bit, one delegation per site. A web service reached over TLS lets a client on a 6to4 address enter its name servers, after checking that they respond and agree, and it can only manage the /48 that matches its own source address.
tldr.outcome: The RFC picks plain, explicit delegation over schemes that alter DNS server behaviour. It admits that address-based authentication is weak and that a reverse mapping should not be trusted. RFC 8996 later updated it.

facts.label: Delegation point
facts.value: The 48th bit position, one per site

facts.label: Periodic check
facts.value: Every 30 days, with a second check 14 days later

today: RFC 5158 is an Informational RFC from March 2008, and it has been updated by RFC 8996. The text says that 6to4 is intended as a transition mechanism useful for a limited period of time in a limited context, and that IANA has delegated the 2.0.0.2.ip6.arpa domain according to delegation instructions provided by the Internet Architecture Board.

sections.title: Why 6to4 Needs Reverse Delegation
sections.content:
6to4 defines a mechanism that lets isolated IPv6 sites communicate using IPv6 over the public IPv4 Internet, through a dedicated IPv6 global unicast address prefix. A 6to4 router can use its IPv4 address value together with that global prefix to create a local IPv6 site prefix, and local IPv6 hosts use the site prefix to form their own IPv6 addresses. The address structure lets any site connected to the IPv4 Internet use IPv6 over automatically created IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnels, so IPv6 can be deployed piece by piece and a local site can reach an IPv6 network without necessarily obtaining IPv6 services from its upstream provider.

The question this memo addresses is setting up the delegations that allow reverse lookups for that address space. A reverse lookup needs a delegation path for the address being queried, from the DNS root to the servers for the zone that provides the PTR records. For ordinary IPv6 addresses those records are maintained by the organisation to which an address block is delegated, so the delegation path mirrors the delegation of address blocks. For IPv6 addresses beginning with the 6to4 prefix the records would need to reflect IPv4 address delegation instead, and since the whole point of 6to4 is to decouple site deployment from infrastructure deployment, such records cannot be expected to be present, especially for a site whose ISP does not support IPv6 at all.

The RFC lists the characteristics a reverse lookup delegation mechanism should have: that it is deployable with minimal overhead or tool development, that it has no impact on existing DNS software and existing DNS operations, that it performs name lookup efficiently, and that it does not compromise any DNS security functions.
sections.plainLanguage: A reverse lookup turns an address back into a name, and it needs the DNS to know which servers hold the records for that address. A 6to4 site's records would have to follow the delegation of its IPv4 address, and its provider may offer no IPv6 service at all, so those records do not exist.

sections.title: The Approaches Considered
sections.content:
The RFC summarises four ways to make reverse lookups work and rejects three of them.

Conventional address delegation has the problem of piecemeal deployment of 6to4 sites. A site uses 6to4 because its upstream provider does not support an IPv6 transit service, and the upstream may be providing no IPv6-based services at all, so it would not be expected to have a 6to4 reverse DNS delegation for its IPv4 address block. Sub-delegations of IPv4 provider address space are also not consistently recorded, so any 6to4 reverse zone operator would have to undertake reverse zone delegations without reliable current address assignment information, undertaking a hop over of the upstream provider's address block, and a delegated entity may need the same hop over when delegating further down.

Guessing a non-delegated server would alter server behaviour so that where no explicit delegation exists in the zone file, the server looks up the in-addr.arpa domain for the servers of the equivalent IPv4 address and queries them for the IPv6 PTR query. The issues with fielding altered server behaviour for this domain are not to be taken lightly, and the delegation chain for IPv4 will not be the same for 6to4 anyway: an isolated 6to4 site uses a single IPv4 /32 address, and it is improbable that a single address would have explicit in-addr.arpa delegation.

Locating local servers at reserved addresses would decode the 6to4 query, rewrite the site-specific part of the address to a constant value and use that as the target of a lookup query. This requires the 6to4 site to reserve local addresses and configure reverse servers on them, and getting DNS to query non-delegated addresses generates spurious traffic.

Synthesized responses would construct a pseudo host name using the IPv6 query address as the seed. Given that the host name has no valid forward DNS mapping, that becomes a case of transforming one invalid DNS object into another.

The conclusion is to support a model of conventional standard delegation, and to reduce the administrative overhead of managing the zone by providing the delegation capability directly to each 6to4 site.
sections.plainLanguage: Four options were considered. Three of them had the DNS server guess where the records are, or make a name up on the spot. The RFC keeps ordinary delegation and lowers the administrative cost by letting each site manage its own entry.

sections.title: How a 6to4 Site Gets Its Prefix
sections.content:
A 6to4 client network is an isolated IPv6 network, made up of a set of IPv6 hosts and a dual-stack local router connected to the local IPv6 network and the external IPv4 network. The IPv4 address used in generating the 6to4 addresses for the local network is the address of the external IPv4 network interface.

The RFC's example: if that interface has the IPv4 address 192.0.2.1, then the local IPv6 clients use a common IPv6 address prefix of the form 2002:{192.0.2.1}::/48, which is 2002:C000:201::/48 in hex notation. All the local IPv6 clients share this common /48 address prefix, irrespective of any local IPv4 address that such a host may use if it is operating in dual-stack mode. The interface identifiers of the clients then complete their addresses, so the examples are 2002:C000:201::1A, ::1B and ::1C.

This is why delegation is done per site: one site corresponds to one /48 prefix and one IPv4 /32 address.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv4 address of the router's outside interface becomes the front part of every IPv6 address in the site. In the RFC's example, 192.0.2.1 produces the site prefix 2002:C000:201::/48, and the hosts differ only in the last part of their address.

sections.title: The Delegation Service
sections.content:
The specification uses a single delegation level in the 2.0.0.2.ip6.arpa zone, delegating zones only at the 48th bit position, which corresponds to individual delegations related to a single /32 IPv4 address, or the equivalent of a single 6to4 local site. The zone files holding the end site delegations are operated with a low TTL, configured to be a time value in the scale of hours rather than days or weeks, and updates for delegation requests are made using dynamic DNS updates.

The delegation system is self-driven by clients residing within 6to4 networks. The function is accessible only by clients using 6to4 IPv6 source addresses, and the only delegation that can be managed is the one corresponding to the /48 prefix of the IPv6 source address of the client. The service operates the delegation management interface as a web server using TLS, reached through an https: URL, which is intended to ensure that the source-address-driven selection cannot be disrupted through proxy caching of the web server's responses and that the delegation service cannot be readily mimicked. The service is to be found at https://6to4.nro.net and is implemented by web servers operated on a dual-stack IPv4 and IPv6 server. If the client uses a 6to4 source address, the server presents a delegation interface for the corresponding 6to4 reverse zone; otherwise it provides a description of the delegation process.

The interface is a conventional DNS delegation interface, allowing the client to enter the details of a number of DNS servers for the corresponding reverse domain. The targets of the delegation are checked by the delegation manager over IPv4 and IPv6, according to the addresses of the targets, to make sure they are responding, that they are configured consistently, and that they are authoritative for the delegated domain. If those conditions are met, the delegation details are entered into the zone at the primary master. To avoid the server being used as a denial of service platform, it should throttle the number of DNS delegation requests made to any single IP address, and also the number of redelegation requests for any single 6to4 zone. In other cases the system provides diagnostic information to the client.

For maintenance, the service keeps an email contact point for each active delegation, derived from the zone's SOA contact address, or explicitly entered in the delegation interface, and informs it of any subsequent change of delegation details. The system also takes a periodic sweep of all active delegations, so that each delegation is checked every 30 days; if a delegation fails the check, the contact point is informed and a further check is scheduled 14 days later, and if that second check fails the delegation is automatically removed and a further notice is issued.
sections.plainLanguage: The service is a web page reached over TLS. A client with a 6to4 source address is shown a form for its own /48 prefix and nothing else. The named servers are checked over IPv4 and IPv6 before the entry is written into the zone, and every entry is re-checked every 30 days.

sections.title: Known Issues and the Conditions for a Delegation
sections.content:
The RFC calls the structure fully automated, delivered on demand, with the system permitting only self-operation of the delegation function, and then lists the potential issues.

Clients inside a 6to4 site could alter the delegation details without the knowledge of the site administrator, which the RFC says is intended for small-scale sites; where that is a concern, the local administrator can take access control measures, in the form of a firewall configuration or a similar mechanism. A 6to4 site with a dynamically assigned external IPv4 interface address could inherit nonsense reverse entries created by previous users of that address, so the RFC recommends using a static IPv4 address in preference to a dynamically assigned one, or updating the delegation through the service on each dynamic address assignment event. The approach does not scale efficiently, because the flat zone file may grow considerably; the RFC notes that 6to4 is intended as a transition mechanism useful for a limited period in a limited context, and estimates the upper bound of the size of the zone at the order of millions of entries, while also noting that the value of a reverse delegation is a questionable proposition and many deployment environments have no form of reverse delegation at all. An enterprise network might decide to use 6to4 internally in a private context, with the hosts visible only in internal DNS servers, in which case the reverse delegation would need to be implemented in an internal, non-delegated zone of the 6to4 reverse domain space.

There may also be circumstances where an IPv4 address controller wishes to block the ability for users of its addresses to use the 6to4 scheme, for example where the provider also offers an IPv6 service and native IPv6 should be deployed instead; the 6to4 reverse zone operator should allow such a blocking function upon application. Three conditions should hold for a delegation to be undertaken: the site must have configured at least one primary and one secondary server for the 6to4 IPv6 reverse address zone; at the time of the request those servers must be online, reachable, correctly configured and in a mutually consistent state, meaning the same SOA record and identical NS record sets; and the service will only accept delegation requests associated with the 6to4 source address of the requesting client.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone inside a 6to4 site can change the entry, and the flat zone file can grow to millions of records. The RFC recommends a static IPv4 address, and notes that 6to4 was only ever meant as a short-lived transition mechanism.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The system offers a rudimentary level of assurance in trying to ensure that delegation requests from a 6to4 site can only direct the delegation of the corresponding 6to4 reverse DNS domain and no other. Address-based authentication is not a very robust method from a security perspective, as addresses can be readily spoofed. Accordingly, reverse delegation information does not provide reliable information either in validating a domain name or in validating an IP address, and no conclusions should be drawn from the presence or otherwise of a reverse DNS mapping for any IP address.

The service management interface allows a 6to4 client to insert any server name as a DNS server, potentially directing the delegation test system to make a DNS query to any nominated system. The server throttles the number of requests made to any single IP address to mitigate the risk of a high volume of bogus DNS queries, and for similar reasons also throttles the number of redelegation requests for any single 6to4 zone. For a general threat analysis of 6to4, especially the additional risk of address spoofing in 2002::/16, the RFC points to RFC 3964.

The RFC also notes that the local site administrator could take access control measures to prevent clients inside a 6to4 site performing unauthorised changes to the delegation details, for example a firewall configuration controlling access to the service from the interior of the site.
sections.plainLanguage: The service trusts the source address of the request, and addresses can be spoofed. The RFC therefore says a reverse entry proves nothing about a name or an address, and that nobody should rely on one being present.

viz.caption: THE FOUR APPROACHES AND WHY THREE WERE REJECTED

cells: Sites delegate their reverse zone the ordinary way
Piecemeal deployment leaves no delegation to follow, so operators must hop over the upstream block
The server looks up the matching in-addr.arpa servers and asks them instead
The IPv4 delegation chain is not the same, and a single /32 is unlikely to be delegated
The query is decoded and rewritten to a constant address
Sites must reserve addresses, and it generates spurious traffic
A pseudo host name is built from the address
The name has no valid forward mapping, so one invalid object becomes another
Each site manages its own delegation through the service
Not rejected; this is what the RFC specifies

viz.caption: THE CONDITIONS FOR A DELEGATION TO BE ACCEPTED

items.title: One primary, one secondary
items.text: The site must have configured at least one primary and one secondary server for its 6to4 reverse zone.

items.title: The servers agree
items.text: Both must be online, reachable, correctly configured and mutually consistent, meaning the same SOA record and identical NS record sets.

items.title: The request matches
items.text: The service accepts only delegation requests associated with the 6to4 source address of the requesting client.
